The roads in the last century which led to War- rington will also account for niacin Writing in 1791 Adam Watk in says that when he crosses the Nlersev for Warrington "we enter now the county for in- ilustry and spirit," hut he also speaks of the rite- advantages which the inhabitants had to struggle against in the matter of roads. The Barley Now is a line example of the latter part of the sixteenth century, and t lie repetition of forms in the quatrefoils is excellent. There is a large room upstairs that is beautifully panelled and ocetipies the whole front overlooking the Alarket Square. The webs are carved in excellent Eliza- bethan style, and they run almost round the great apartment that commands a view of the entire sqltare. Before the new market was built in the mita, the country people hid out their goods under stalls such 18 we Ser. now in Continental towns, and the square shadowed by old-fashioned dwellings was extremely picturesque. " TOUCH AND U(,: j New Reading.) The "Times- is out of joint! 0 mimed spite, Sinai l'igott was not born to net it tight.
Why is Pigott like the last comet? Bemuse, although lie has disappeared, he is "forging" his way somewhere.

1, "Father Stephens was arrested at Falcarragh, on Sanday. shortly after celebrating Mass, by a warrant under the Crimes Act." A man named Ryan was summoned before the Liverpool magistrates oil Monday, for allowing his horse and trap to remain in the street "during an unnecessary period:. It transpired that part of the peri.l was occupied in treating the Constable who reported the case to a glass of rum. This was too moth for the Bench; they dismissed the ease. P.C. 1092 has evidently a rum idea of his duty. .

! A London Correspondent, after referring, 1111 leSday, toa vague rumour that Pigott had lwen !assassinated said--" There is, however, no doubt : that Dr. Maguire, whose name figured prominently in w ome of the earlier evidence, has died. It WM Dr. Mffiviire who backed up Houston in his traffic With Pigott, and even found some of the money with which the forged letters were purchased. His death has added a fresh sensation to those that crowd around the case."

A lad named John Fisher, recently employed at the works of Messrs. Monks,Hall,and Co., has hem remanded on a charge if wilfully damaging machinery. It is stated that he threw a .pful of sand into the machinery, as he " wanted to play " while the mischief he had done was being act right. Ho is likely to get play enough : nobody will employ him if he continuo to repeat his perform- ance. Hy way of breaking him oil ii bad habit, he ought to Ire net to work on the treadmill.

The traders of Warrington did well to meet rn Monday, and let it be seen that they are alive to !their .iwn interests. It is evident that the flail- way Companies have IM eye to the inain chance !wheit, under the new Railways Act, they propose changes which may mean an increase of from 50 Ito MO per cent. Railway Companies may not , insist on the maximum charges ; but on the other • hand they may. The safest plan is to draw the lion's teeth before venturing one's head betweim its jaws.

All good Liberals rejoice in the tribute to Mr. ilenry Dunckley, or Dr. Dunaley as he is now called, on the euverance of his long imunection with the Mnichester Examiner." Hu has been " the bright particular star" of Lancashire journalism for many years, and has done much in dark days and troubkins times to encourage those who were struggling in, toilsome path. It is to be hoped that this writer of the letters of Verax" will continue to enlighten and charm his ever- widening circle of admirers.

The "Times " has withdrawn the letters about ! which it has shrieked so 1111 l ch, and has apologised to Mr. Parnell It is true that the apology is neither veryf rank nor very gracious ; it is cramped by the knowledge that there will be numerous actions for libels, with consequent heavy damages. If the " Times " had not been so bitter and so ' cot4eure, one could pity it. Its collapse is appall- ing ; but its stupidity nes been appalling. It has been led by prejudice and passion, and they are both blind guides.
Speaking at Derby, on Wedmadav, Sir William Harcourt showed up the folly of the Times." He said :

1-TXrisli I had known Mr. Pigott was at the bottom of this concern. Why everybody except TA* Dews newspaper, I suppose, and my poor good- natured friend Mr. Forster knew all about Mr. Pigott. Why he wrote to me over and over again-- (laughter) -when I war in office efferiug to sell .re everything and everybody—but I was not such a greenhorn —(load laughter) as the managers of The Tense or her Majesty's Attorney-General. (Laughter and cheers.) The first question that occurred to me to ask was one which never appears to have occurred to them, namely, Who is Mr. Pigott? Well, everybody told me at once, Iles a disrepmable, broken-down Irish journalist. Don't touch him with o ruarlinspike.' (Laughter and cheers.)

A girl named Heiner, 14 years of ago, was buried under a load of straw which fell upon her at Earlestown, on Monday afternoon. It was feared that she would be killed, but the force of the fall was broken by some pilings, and she was got out • without auffering serious injury. The accident is , one which suggests the need of better provision . for the protection of life. Ships have a load line ; and a hue might to be drawn in loading carts with hay and straw. To the uninitiated, there carts always seem, like vaulting ululation, to be on the , point of toppling over on the other side. The new Bishop of Chester was consecrated at , York oil Sunday. Consecration is a more serious bminess than that of election. Describing the r latter process, Emerson, in his Essay on Religion, says;—" The bishop is elected by the Dean and Prebends of the cathedral. The Queen sends these gentleinen a ',nye% Jelin., or leave to elect ; but also sends the mom of the person whom they are to elect. They g., into the cathedral, chant, and pray and beseech the Holy Ghost to visit thorn in ; their choice; and, after these invocations, invari- ably find that the dictates of the Holy Ghost agree with the recominendatioo of the Queen." The Rev. Henry Me-y M-ell preached at the War- ; rington Parish Church, 01 Stinclay, on behalf of : middle-class schools to " provide a thoroughly good education Mr the soon ni any man who could say, eightempence a day for that purpose." —• There mass very large audience at the above on Monday Evening. The concert was promoted for the purpose of raising funds for the purchase of a magic lantern to instruct and amuse the children who attend these schools. The chair was taken by Mr. McDougall, who said before calling upon the vocalists he would give a few statistics with regard ' to the amount of work done in these schooLs. At the prment moment there were no fewer than 281 boys on' the rolls of attendance. Last year them was 175, there-1 fore them was :tti actual increase within two years of 180. (Applause.) Considering that, he thought they 1 would agree with him that was is wry interesting record. Tile average atiendanee in the boys' scissd was 243, whilst I.st year it was 140 only. In the girls' school the number on the rolls was 237, as companal with PM last year, oran increase of 71. The average attendance was 190, last year 103. To the friends of education that most be extremely satisfactory and agreeable information. (Applause.) an instrumental selection by the Mrssrs. Guest was the tind item on the prognonme, and this, together with the two other given during the evening by them, were most enjoyable. Miss Simkin sang with marked expres- sion "Alone on the raft " ; aad Mr Morris gave in capital style "I fear no foe." Miss Joynson, who hails from Northwich, sang "Someone's little sweetheart," and " Love's golden dream," with much feeling, and for which she received a well merited encore. "The Shadow of the Cross," and "An old garden," were splendidly rendered by Miss rierpoint, and she was Isilly ap- plauded. Mr. John Ilirkett gave with gnnt gusto " Anch dal,' and also ably assisted in the glee "Here's a health unto Isis Majesty," and in the trio "To shepherds tell ne," Mr. Williams and Mr. Morris taking ;ma in both the latter. div.head: HUXLEY'S AGNOSTICISM . By Ivsx.
div.p: HUXLEY'S AGNOSTICISM . By Ivsx.

Professor i-chr--Oti Agnosticism in the " Contemporary Review " will hardly add to the , celebrity of that eminent scientist. The deep gees- ' thins with which Agnosticism is more properly con- Honed are practically ignored, and the Profesmr, after the manlier of •• Hall of Science " Orators, I disposes of the miraculous by apparently showing a balance of probability. against what he bluntly terms the " (Ware. tog story." That portion of the ;midi+ which is not occopied with t lie treatment of historical problemo by a method applicable only to physical, or possibly, natural, science, is devoted to the pummeling of Mr. Frederic Harrison for his audacity in cornering Agnostics on the question of religion in the " Fortnightly" for January. The Professor, who first gave currency to the term Agnosticism, which signifies without knowledge, could hardly read the following without feeling exceedingly wroth with the High Priest of Posi- tivism Until Agnosticism has told us," said Mr. Harrison, .• what religion we are to believe, or why religion is henceforth superfluous, it will remain the opinion of isolated and cultivated minds in more or less comfortable surroundings." And again i--" The Agnostic is willing to trust to science as an adequate answer to the in- tellect, to ethics as a sufficient basis for con- duct." Ile might as well trust in the " rule of three and in the maxims in a ropy book' to carry him through the storms of life. If any- one should inquire of Mr. Harrison what religion he refers to, the Bremer will be that in the service and worship of Humanity be will and all the con- notation and prospective happiness hitherto ignor- antly supposed to bo the peculiar gift of Christian- ity. The religion of Po.sitivism is surely a miserable delusion. What possible attraction can there be in , the rag-tag and bobtail of all ages, of all nations— 1 the filthy, lewd, barbarous civilized, ignorant wise, vicious—grouped under a glittering generalization. If such an idol is capable of producing feelings akin to those of pure religion, they are probably tbe result of morality, touched not with emotion, but by hysteria. Shall Vel: follow Huxley and dis- pense with religion,or Harrison and deify ourselves? Or will it be better for us to bow before the shrine of the Unknowable, and accept the ministratiomi of Mr. Spencer who can teach us how to know tire, unknowable? shall we adopt Pantheism, mid gaze with breathless adoration on the "Queen of the heavenly lutes," make vows by the golden stars of heaven, and from a meditation on the glories of eternal sunsets, find strength and consolation for the weary toil of life ? One thing in certain, until the anti-christian thought in less divided against itself it will scarcely come with any commendation to the millions engaged in the strife and toil of

-Tn.:lessor Huxley's Agnosticism is neither more nor lees than the exaltation of reason above, and, if 1 needs be, in defiance of every other human faculty. ' "It is net a creed, bnt a method, the essence of which lies in the application of a single principle," which principle is,—. In matters of intellect follow your reason as far no it will take you without regard to any other conoideration ; . . . . and do not pretend that conclusions are certain which are not demonstrated or demonstrable." If this be Agnosticism, then there are more Agnostics than is commonly imagined. Every school-boy working a problem of Euclid, every Sell. A-girl puzzling out Rule of Three, are for the time being, Agnostics, inasmuch as they are following their reason in "matters of intellect." If by Agnosticism nothing more is intended than is above explicitly stated,then the term ion brilliant mi,nomer. But the point is , to be found in the tacit assumption that loyalty to reason will lead men to non-belief in God, immortal- ity, and all that appertains thereto. Now it may be reinarked that the above " method" IP purely a personal one. Hod man an infallible reason then possibly good results would accrue but even then it would be utterly impracticable for the vast majority of men to follow their reason in "matters • f intellect under moot circumstances. For men to become Agnostic* by . adopting Professor linxley's principle would mean ! the creation of as many social,politicaLscientific,and • religious modes of thought as there would be think- Mg men. No man could he a consistent Agnostic in this sense ; he would have to take much of hie , • knowledge on authority, else die ignorant. . Again: "In matters of intellect," we are to follow ' our reason. Are there, then," matters" which nave, no relation to tlm intellect? If none then when i reason leads as to the belief in a Personal Ruler of the universe hare we become Agnostics? If there , are, then reason is clearly ruled out of coin t in all , matters saving those relating to the intellect. If t religion is a " matter of intellect;' then reason may, as it does in many COMS, strengthen our roam- - tions regarding the great religious verities ; if it is not a "matter of intellect," Professor Huxley 's • scieetitic 17 ritici,m is futile, out of the place, and unscientific.

...... s. : The Agnostic attitude will not permit on to be "certain" of anything which is not either demon- strated or demonstrable. Professor Huxley holds the opinion that life originated in non-living matter. In he " certain' that bin opinion is correct? It cannot be demonstrated. Scientific experiments conducted by some of the keenest observers in Europe show conclusively that life can only conic from pre-exist ing life. Ile is, therefore, either " certain" about that which is incapable of demonstration, or, he holds an opinion on a momentous subject of which he is not certain. The same reasoning in applicable to other scientill.• beliefs, r. y.,the Atomic theory, and the existence of Ether. Now if Professor Maley has opinions or beliefs regatiling scientific matters, the truth of which is scientifically undemonstrable, surely a religious thinker may bold a religious belief, even though such belief incapable of scientific Ilemon- stration. But to whom demonstrable? Different men require and are satisfied with various degrees of proof glad a man may be &Min flint he loves bin wife or children without being able to prove it wientifically to himself or to others. Again : What arewe to think of the following front it thinker who demands scientific demonstra- tion as the condition of certainty ? "I repeat with- out the slightest fear of refutation, that the four , Gospels, an they have come to us, are the work of, unknown anthers.' One would have thotight to : and the Professor,who admits to having "nil preten- sion to being an expert ' in historical ntatters, a little less dogmatic on a subject of which he Can- not but he an incompetent judge. Gin also interest- ing to know that "what Jesus said and did i, strictly a scientific problem." This is certainly something new. Perhaps in a few yeant time the Theological Colleges will accept the Professoia

The Oil for veterinary purposes is placed in yellow wrappers and is quite a different thing from the Oil in white wrappers. The former contains ingredients particularly adapted for use on animals, and is far superior to all other liniments and embrocations for veterinary purposes. The public are particularly cautioned to use the Oil in yellow wrappers only for veterinary purposes. The price of the Oil is within the reach of all, viz., two shillings and sixpence per bottle, of all dealers in veterinary medicines, or free by parcels post from the proprietors. We should most certainly say, from the enormous popularity which the Oil has attainizl, not only in this country but in every part of the civilised world, that no stabio or kerniel will be complete without St. Jacobs Oil in yellow wrappers. It is now used extensively and with wonderful success by the leading. Job- Masters, Omnibus and Cab Companies of London and provincial cities, an all cases where an outward application is indicated. The West-End Omnibus Company, of Auckland, Ness Zealand, of which Mr. S. Child is manager, writes to the Daily licie'd of that cite:—” We have much pleasure in bearing testimony to the efficacy of St. Jacobs Oil in yellow wrappers for veterinary purposes. Its success has been particularly marked in cases of lame- ness in our stables. For man and beast, St. J. .....Oil is the greatest pain-cure ever discovered. Perhaps there is no preparation in the world which enjoys the same degree of success and popularity as St. Jacobs Oil. Its sale far exceeds that of any other Proprietary Medicine, and exceeds by ten times that of all other liniments and embrocations combined. This wonderful success rests on the solid foundation of merit which St. Jacobs Oil possesses, combined with original, dignified, and systematic advertising, which has always characterised the announcements of the Proprietors. The name "St. Jacobs Oil" has become a household word in every civilised country in the world. The great success and popularity of the Oil has become the subject of comment by almost the entire Press of the country. Sir,—Kindly permit me to draw attention toll prac- tice that some people have of taking liberties with books they have borrowed from the Leading Library. It is nothing uocommon to snd books issued from the library with passages underlined in pencil, and in many instant,lu with remarks wribbled on the side of someof the pages, expressing the writer's approval or disap- proval of certain sentiments, or opinions in regent to chomaws pourtrayed by the author. Some people may consider that bocause they obtain the use of a book fora penny they can deface it in any svay they like, but I think the practice a very objectionable one, and with just to mention it by way of protest. As it is no doubt done in thoughtlessness, perhaps this word of region. straw,. may have some effect.—Yours truly, A HEADER.

Certainly football is not a gently game and does not tend naturally I. develop gentle manners. All the more reason that our players shonld be on their guard against any offence agabot good manners, whether during a match or after it. I have watched many games at Preoat and have been quite pleased to note the restraint put by our M. Ofl themselves under trying circumstances. When cricket first became popular there were equally hard things said and with Justice ; but now nobody thinks of throw- ing ill2l bat at the head of the Umpire who has given him out I.b.w. Yet! never knew a man who agreed: with the umpire under these circumstances. Our Bible ! Clam football eleven promises to become a leading one ! in this district. I feel sure that it will continue to deserve ! ! the good name it has already won and than give an ! i eallSe to be proud of it. Yours Sm., HARRY MITCHELL, Vicar of rrescot. THE IRISH QUESTION.

Sir,—Will you kindly allow or a little space in the ' columns of your newspaper, as it is really time for every man who loves liberty and freedom of speech, to speak out and protest against this Tory Government. They have filled the land with soldiers and police and all kinds of base informers,who are always ready to sell anytiody. I now give a sainfee of Mr. Halfour's grave-yards in Ireland :—Patrick ()Mani., murdered by the police at Yougliall, April, 1887; Michael bonergan, inurdereil by the police at Afitchelstown, September 9th, 1887 ; John Shinnick, inurdered by the pollen at Mitchelstown. Sep- tember 9th, 1887; John Casey, murdered by the pollee at Mitchelstown. September 1887; John Kinsella, murdered by emergency men at Coolgnmay, September 28111, 1887; Thomas Larkin. unuttered in Kilkenny jail, September 27th, 1887; likewise tlw late John Mandevelle, ; whom Italfiam's government drove than untimely grave. They first try to gag the people, and when they cannot do that to their satisfaetion they try all kinds of brutal remedies. It is lamentable to read; week after week, of the large emigration from he shores 'if Ireland, when the land could maintain from 15 to 20 million, of good industrious people by means of Ilona. Rule, which is certain to come. I hope and trust that England's noblest and bravest son will accomplish it—l mean William Ewart Gladstone. Now, sir, I wish to say some- thing about the landlords of Ireland. About 10,000 of them own 15,000,000 acme of land, and these men ex- tract enough to beggar any country. The late Mr. John Stuart Mill, declared that the ladd of Ireland, like the laud of every other country, belongs to the people who inhabit it, and wken her people are forced to leave the land in thoumnds, the Government is already com cicumed,—Tnno - -

Sir,—An many of your readers are not aware of the instruction now being given to candidates for confirma- tion, with your kind permission I would draw their attention to the following pamphlets now in use. No. 1, " Parochial Papern," by the Bishop of Lichfield, in which it says, " It is Christ Himself we receive in Holy Communion—Christ Himself and nothing less. And in Rim all things. Ile is preennt there to give us flimsolf." What is this but Transubstantiation, as opposed to Articles 28 and 31, wherein we read the bread and wine are taken only after a spiritual manner by faith, and the offering of Christ once made is the perfect redemp- tion, propitiation and satisfaction ; Acts 3,t, 21v. ; fink 10c.. 10, 12, 14v. Confirmation paper by Rev. M. F. Sadler says, "For what purpose does the Bishop by his hands on those to be oonfinned That they mav he strengthened with the Holy Ghost." {that tragh ! The Bible says, "God giveth the Holy Spirit to them that ask Him," Luke lie., 13v. A Bishop not long since mid if any one expected the Holy Spirit they would to get it through such men as himself. The laying on of hands, he says, was a sacramental rite upon those who had hivn baptised. This is further rubbish, for Mathias wan Amen by the assembly by lot. Acts 1c.,15, 26v.; and Saint Paul received the Holy Ghost before he was baptised and without any laying on of hands of the apostles, bishops, or elders. Mr. Sadler says it ins very great sin to reject layingon of hands, because God ordained ronllnnation,that in it Christiam should receive the Holy Spirit. This I dispute it is a rite of man's creation, tlie same as ordination of Itishorw. Presbyters, he.. to support their priestcraft. The word " ordain " eorrectlytranslated It" made" or" appoint" Rev. Sc., ; Matt. 25c., 21v.; Luke 125., 14v. The N. T. revisers have seen through this trickery and give the right word. Mr. Sadler. according to tine" English Churchman." of Oct. 27,1887, teaches. " Priestly abso- lution, baptismal regeneration, the real presence, andthe sacrificial character of the Lonl's Sapper in a I way which no loyal churchman maid tolerate." Fellow townsmen, are you going to sit still and allow your children to be contaminated with such per- nicioug instruction? There is nothing sound about it. lithe Vicar of Runcorn expects any real spiritual good mit of such chaff, he may expect to reap a whirlwind. lithe Church is not mended the democracy will end it. Certain would-be primts, traitors or Jesuits in disguise, are doing the work of Rome better than she can do it, aye, even with Protestant money. Thee men would probably like to see the Canon laws in force, one of which says, "Whatever decrees of princes are found injurious to Line interests of the Church are declared tobe of no authority whatever." I would conclude in the noble words the late Dean of Ripon, Hugh McNeil.. "Freeborn Englishmen be wise, be firin, deliver your country, your beloved country, unequalled on the globe; 0 delirer her, and keep her delivered, decidedly and no mistake, from the despotic grasp of Antichrist," from the iron chain of the Canon law. Frodsham, Feb. 20,1689.

NORTHWICH DIVISION LIBERAL ASSOCIATION. ANNUAL MEETING.

The annual meeting of the members of the Gen- eral Council of this Association wan held in the Primitive Methodist school, Nortn win!), on Satur- day afternoon. There was. good attendance, repre- sentatives being present from all parts of the divi- sion. The members from Runcorn were the Rev. K Hall, Messrs. T. Handley, J. Clark, R. Moore, T. Clegg, J. Pickering, W. Betney, J. Jones, J. N'aulk- ner, J. Bridgewater, K Wynne llumplireys. Bellamy. W. Carroll, W. Norman, and W. llandley, (General Secretary). In the absence of the Presi- dent, Mr. B. Milner, of Northwich, was voted to the chair.

s The Secretary mad his annual H. which stated that though they had not had the stinsulas of an I election as in the three former yeam the record of the labours of the past twelve months would prove that the aim and purpose of the Association had been kept in view, and useful work accomplished. At the titne of the last annual meeting. Parliament had just suet, and had announced that the measure of the year would be a Local Government Bill for England and Wales. A letter was read from Mr. Brunner suggesting theconsideration of the Bill by the Asseciation and that the views of the members should be forwarded for his guidance as their representative. This communication was referred to the Executive, who at once appointed a committee con- sisting of represontatives front all parts of the division tO 01.111410 and report upon it. This committee sat on April 21st, and after careful examination, embodied their suggestions in al report to the Executive meeting held May 12th, which report was slightly amended and adopted, and forwarded to Mr. Brunner. It is satis- factory to note that so many of the suggestions were incorporated by way of amendment to he Bill, and the thanks of the Association are due to their humoured representative for the untiring interest he took in the measure and his mastery of its details, which enabled him to introduce and carry several valuable amend- ments ere the Bill fit:ally became the law of the land. (Applause). The whole country was roused by the so called Compensation Clauses, , and so unanitnonsly had the Government's mons, rous proposals been condemned that they withdrew them and a demonstration held in Winnington Park on June 181 t became a sort of Doxology. (Laughter and applause.) The next meeting of the Executive was held at Wintnng. ton Hall on September Ist, and the arrangements were there made for Mr. Brunner visiting his constituents and delivering addresses during the mouth in the tour towns of the Division—Middlewieh, Northwieh, Runcorn, and Winston!. Such an arrangement was unknown in Cheshire in the "good old days," but a dem:wrath: suffrage not only makes it necessary but wise,and to our member it was not only a duty but a sincere pleasure. (Applause.) The next Executtve meeting was held on the 18t1, October, at which their Secretary presented the , report of the registration work. Thii work had been much more difficult and onerous owing to the passing of the County Electors Act, rendered necessary for the , election of the new County Councils. as it introduced , new franchises, and the various provisions with regard therto were as confusing that few of the township offi- , vials understood the changes which went so hurriedly and compulsorily introduced into the old order et things. The number of claims madn by the agents of the Associa- tion were greatly in excess of former years in many townships, owing to the numerous omissions from the lists of thase fully qualified, and had it not bmn for the lean:exert:l.A a large number would have been disquali- fied. a consequence. At the recent high tides the water flooded the marsh and almost surinountisl the embankments and imindated the rutting. It has therefore been deemed advisable to increase the height of the embankments and this is being done. div.head: RUNCORN.
div.p: RUNCORN.

Great activity In being displayed on this section. At the Norton end the construction of the Randall sluices is being rapidly proceeded with, the work of putting in the masonry having now commenced. While at No Man's Land good progress is being made with the building of the river wall. Immense quantities of concrete and red sandstone have no far been used in its construction. Above Runcorn Bridge great interest is centred in the pile driving operation.s. Two power- ful steam pile drivers are now employed, one of which is capable of working at low tide, and each dayhundreds view the scene from the bridge. The piles net huge : beams of timber aimed 40 feet in length, and these are ••riven into the &Intl a depth of about 25 feet. About •80 of these Idles have now been fixed, and a second row parallel, with the tee has been commenced. ACCIDENT AT WESTON POINT.

; On Monday, I. Lynn., a foreman employed in the ; rnnstruction of the great lock at Weston Point, met with a serious accident. Ile was superintending the mixing of concrete and gravel, when a wagon was Icing lowered : into the excavations, and the chain of the crane coming . in contact with him, threw him from his position, and . ;he fell a distance of 31 feet. He was very badly shaken, and was injured on the luck, neck and wrist. As , quickly as possible he wad removed to the hut and He. McDougall was sent for, and under that grntlenian's ; care he Is provresslng favourably. NEW MISSION HALL AT RUNCORN. ! On Sunday a new Hldp finial Mission Hall, diluted in ' lisvell4ane,lluncorn, was opened by the Hon. and Hey. It. Grimston M.A. Twelve months agn when Mr. Watson, the missionary, commenced his labour amongst the ; navvies and ether workmen on the Runevirn section, the : Mariner's Church in Irwell-lane was rented for the purpose of holding services, but the success that attem ded his labours was so grvat that it soon became evident the accommodation provided was far from adequate. With characteristic thoroughness Mr. Walker at once contract.' with Messrs. Thomas Kirkham and Co., for the construction of a new building, and the latter firm are to be cmnplimented upon the expedition with whirn they have accomplished their task. The new building is al corrugated iron, lined on the inside with match board- ing. The space between the outside and the inside bring filled with sand and sawdust, by this Jima,ns the building is kept dry and free from draughts. In dimen- sions the building is 80 feet long by 40 feet wide, accommodation being provided for about 500 persons. At the east end of the structure are two rlassrooms, which can converted into one room by means of a movable screen, and the arrangements are altogether satisfactory and complete. Both naturally and artifici- rally the light is admirable, and the heating apparatus has been fixed by Messrs. Lea and Son, of High-nt., whose system has been found to work with the utmost advantage. The whole of the furniture is pitchpine, and the appearaneeof the room is altogether bright and cheer- ful. As previously stated the opening services were held on Sunday alien Mr. Grimston preacheff two sermons to large congregation.s. Tho musical nornon of the services was conducted by Mr. Sharrock, who unaided at the powerful American organ with which the mission issup- plied. On Tuesday evening a tea party was held and nearly 300 persons sat down to the excellent tea provided. The tall, were presided over by Mesdames Watson, Graham, Forster, Ashford, Greaves, 3. Brown, Edwards, Wright, and W. Irons; Misses Smith, Forster, and Ashford. Afterwards a public inwting was held and was swell attended. The proceedings were opened by Mr. T. Waddington, missionary of No. 5 section offering ; up prayer, and afterwards the Chairman like Hey. W. Preston, M.A., vicar of Holy Trinity) delivered a char- acteristic speech. Addresses were also given by the , Hon and Rev. R. (irimston. M.A., Mrs. C. Garnett (of Ripon) and Mr. Smith. Mr. Watson, the missionary, ' also spoke and gas, a verbal report of the work of the miwion during the past year, stating that nearly 12,000 persons had attended the servi... Appropriate hymns ! were sung by those present. and the choir rendend an , I anthem in capital style. Miss Forster sang " Flowers ! that fate" and Mrs. Walton" Gates of the West," both ladles being heartily applauded.—The customary vote I of thanks eoneluded the proceedings. On Wednesday evening, the children of the workmen WITI! provided r with a substantial tea and afterwards Mr. H. W. • Handley gave a magic lantern entertainment entitled • "The Life of General Gordon" the views being of a highly interesting character. Appropriate recitations • were 'given by Mtister Wright and Miss tin-naves. The • proceislings were conducted by Mn. Watson, the miwitinary.

! Mr. Parnell claims £50,000 damages for libel in his !action against the 'Times' in the Dublin Court. !Wttlioo Higg, sentenced to death at Durham, will be !hanged on Monday, the 18th inst. This makes the third execut len at Durham tut that day. Notices were on Friday morning served by miners upon all the crwlowners throughout the South Wales and Monminehshire cauf &In for an sale:nice in wages of 12i per cent. A report is current in the law courts that the Parnell Commission has already made one notable convert to Home Rule. This is Mi. Justice Hawkins, who was a strong Unionist. . . _ .
The inward-bound steamer Telephone came into collision at the entrance to the Mersey on Thursday night with the schmner PoHie Williams. The later sank, arid the captain was drowned.
THE ORMSBY FISHING FLEET.-OVER 70 FISHER- MEN DROWNED. _ .

The full results of the dreadful gale on the 9th ult, to the Grimsby fish trade are now becoming known, and of the safety of eight of the miming smacks all hope lam been abandoned. 'Plies, vessels are the British Work- man, Eton, Sir Frederick Roberts, Kitten, Se a Searcher, British Tar, John Wintrinitham, and Harold. The total nutnber of lives lost will reach between 70 and 80. and of vessels to 15 or 18. This calamity to a single port is one of the most appalling on record. THE PARNELL COMMISSION.

At the Special Commission on Friday, Mr. Houston attended to make a personal statement, but the Presi- dent would not admit it.—Mr. Henry Campbell denied the authenticity of the alleged Parnell and Egan letters. —Mr. O'Kelly and Mr. Davitt also repudiated the letters attributed to thetri.—Mr. Lewis said that at the inter- views at Mr. Labouchere's Pigott admittod that the letters were forgeries.—Mr. Laboucherc said he never offered Pigott £l,OOO to swear he was a forger, but he offered to buy any documents he might have ; £l,OOO was then mentioned. Witness described Pigott's last visit and etinfession.—Mr. Sala corroborated.—Mr. Lewis said that at the interview of October the 26th last, Pigott admitted to Mr. Parnell and himself that he was the forger.—Sir Charles Ruxsell asktel the Bench to give their opinion about the lettert.—The President said they would consider that by Tutsday. They could not now go into the question whether there noon foul conspiraey behind Houston.—The Attomey-tieneral then read long extracts from the "Irish World!'
